summary.text: The proof merges the three point families \(n/5\), \(n/\varphi\), and \(n/(1/\varphi)\), using the irrationality of \(\varphi\) (and \(1/\varphi=\varphi-1\)) to show that no two points coincide. Their cumulative floor count increases by exactly one at each successive point, so its ranks exhaust the positive integers without repetition; identifying the three rank formulas with the given sequences yields the partition.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad t=\frac1\varphi.
\]
Thus \(\varphi>0\), \(t>0\), and
\[
\varphi^2=\varphi+1,\qquad \frac1\varphi=\varphi-1.
\]
We consider the three sequences, indexed by positive integers \(n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{n\varphi}{5}\right\rfloor
       +\left\lfloor\frac{nt}{5}\right\rfloor,\\
b(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{\varphi}\right\rfloor
       +\left\lfloor\frac{nt}{\varphi}\right\rfloor,\\
c(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{t}\right\rfloor
       +\left\lfloor\frac{n\varphi}{t}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are A207672, A207673, and A208326, respectively. Since \(t=1/\varphi\), the last formula can equivalently be written
\[
c(n)=n+\lfloor 5n\varphi\rfloor+\lfloor n\varphi^2\rfloor,
\]
which is the stated formula for A208326. We prove that the ranges of \(a,b,c\) are pairwise disjoint and that their union is exactly the set of positive integers.

The proof proceeds by jointly ranking three families of real numbers.

Define
\[
d_0=5,\qquad d_1=\varphi,\qquad d_2=t=\frac1\varphi.
\]
All three \(d_i\) are positive. For \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\) and \(n\ge 1\), put
\[
v_i(n)=\frac{n}{d_i}.
\]
Thus the three families of points are
\[
\left\{\frac n5:n\ge1\right\},\qquad
\left\{\frac n\varphi:n\ge1\right\},\qquad
\left\{\frac n{1/\varphi}:n\ge1\right\}.
\]
We first show that no two of these points coincide unless both their family and their index coincide.

We use the irrationality of \(\varphi\). For completeness, \(\sqrt5\) is irrational: if \(\sqrt5=p/q\) in lowest terms with positive integers \(p,q\), then \(p^2=5q^2\), so \(5\mid p\); writing \(p=5r\) then gives \(q^2=5r^2\), hence \(5\mid q\), contrary to lowest terms. Consequently \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\) is irrational. In particular, if integers \(u,v\) satisfy
\[
u\varphi=v,
\]
then \(u=v=0\): if \(u\ne0\), this equation would make \(\varphi=v/u\) rational, while if \(u=0\), the equation gives \(v=0\).

Within one family, \(v_i(n)=v_i(m)\) implies \(n=m\), because \(d_i>0\). Between distinct families, suppose throughout that \(n,m\ge1\).

First, if
\[
\frac n5=\frac m\varphi,
\]
then \(n\varphi=5m\), impossible because the preceding integer linear relation would force \(n=0\).

Second, if
\[
\frac n5=\frac m{1/\varphi}=m\varphi,
\]
then \(n=5m\varphi\), again impossible because \(5m\ne0\).

Third, if
\[
\frac n\varphi=\frac m{1/\varphi}=m\varphi,
\]
then \(n=m\varphi^2\). Using \(\varphi^2=\varphi+1\), this becomes
\[
(n-m)=m\varphi,
\]
which is impossible because \(m\ge1\). Thus all the points \(v_i(n)\), over all three families and all positive indices, are distinct.

We now establish the ranking principle that drives the proof. For \(x\ge0\), define
\[
C(x)=\sum_{k=0}^2\lfloor d_kx\rfloor.
\]
For each fixed \(k\), the positive integers \(r\) satisfying
\[
v_k(r)=\frac r{d_k}\le x
\]
are exactly \(r=1,2,\ldots,\lfloor d_kx\rfloor\). Hence \(\lfloor d_kx\rfloor\) is the number of points from family \(k\) that are at most \(x\). Since the three families have no common points, \(C(x)\) is exactly the number of points in their joint union that are at most \(x\).

In particular, define the rank of \(v_i(n)\) by
\[
R_i(n)=C(v_i(n))=\sum_{k=0}^2
\left\lfloor d_k\frac n{d_i}\right\rfloor.
\]
This is its position in the increasing joint ordering, with the least point having rank \(1\). We will prove directly that every positive integer occurs as one of these ranks and that no rank occurs twice.

For the covering assertion, fix \(x\ge0\). The first point of family \(k\) strictly larger than \(x\) is
\[
y_k(x)=\frac{\lfloor d_kx\rfloor+1}{d_k}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
d_kx<\lfloor d_kx\rfloor+1,
\]
so \(x<y_k(x)\), and the numerator \(\lfloor d_kx\rfloor+1\) is a positive integer because \(d_kx\ge0\). Every later point in family \(k\) is at least \(y_k(x)\).

Let
\[
y(x)=\min\{y_0(x),y_1(x),y_2(x)\}.
\]
Then \(y(x)>x\), and \(y(x)\) is itself a point in one of the three families. Moreover, precisely one of the three candidates realizes this minimum. If two distinct candidates were equal, they would be equal points belonging to distinct families, contradicting the noncollision result above.

Suppose the unique minimizing family is \(j\), so that \(y(x)=y_j(x)\). For that family,
\[
d_jy(x)=\lfloor d_jx\rfloor+1,
\]
and therefore
\[
\lfloor d_jy(x)\rfloor=\lfloor d_jx\rfloor+1.
\]
For \(k\ne j\), uniqueness of the minimum gives
\[
y(x)<y_k(x)=\frac{\lfloor d_kx\rfloor+1}{d_k}.
\]
On the other hand \(y(x)>x\). Multiplying these inequalities by the positive number \(d_k\) yields
\[
\lfloor d_kx\rfloor\le d_kx<d_ky(x)<\lfloor d_kx\rfloor+1.
\]
Consequently
\[
\lfloor d_ky(x)\rfloor=\lfloor d_kx\rfloor
\qquad(k\ne j).
\]
Exactly one summand in \(C\) has therefore increased by one, and the other two have not changed. Thus
\[
C(y(x))=C(x)+1.
\]

Starting with \(x_0=0\), recursively set
\[
x_{p+1}=y(x_p)\qquad(p\ge0).
\]
Since \(C(0)=0\), induction using the preceding equality gives
\[
C(x_p)=p
\]
for every \(p\ge0\). Also, for every \(p\ge1\), the construction of \(y\) shows that \(x_p\) is one of the special points: there are some \(i\in\{0,1,2\}\) and \(n\ge1\) for which
\[
x_p=v_i(n).
\]
It follows that
\[
p=C(x_p)=C(v_i(n))=R_i(n).
\]
Thus every positive integer \(p\) occurs as the rank of a point in one of the three families.

We next show that such a representation of a rank is unique. More generally, if
\[
v_i(n)<v_j(m),
\]
where \(n,m\ge1\), then
\[
C(v_i(n))<C(v_j(m)).
\]
Indeed, because every \(d_k\) is positive,
\[
d_kv_i(n)\le d_kv_j(m)
\]
for every \(k\), so each floor summand in \(C(v_i(n))\) is at most the corresponding summand in \(C(v_j(m))\). For the particular family \(j\), the inequality is strict enough to force a strict floor increase: since
\[
d_jv_j(m)=m
\]
and \(d_jv_i(n)<m\), we have
\[
\lfloor d_jv_i(n)\rfloor<m
 =\lfloor d_jv_j(m)\rfloor.
\]
Therefore the whole sum is strictly smaller.

Now suppose
\[
R_i(n)=R_j(m).
\]
If \(v_i(n)<v_j(m)\), the preceding result would give \(R_i(n)<R_j(m)\), a contradiction. The reverse strict inequality is equally impossible. Hence
\[
v_i(n)=v_j(m).
\]
By the noncollision result, this forces \(i=j\) and \(n=m\). Thus each positive rank belongs to exactly one family and one index.

It remains to identify these ranks with the three sequences in the statement. For family \(0\), where \(d_0=5\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_0(n)
&=\left\lfloor5\frac n5\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\varphi\frac n5\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor t\frac n5\right\rfloor\\
&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{n\varphi}{5}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{nt}{5}\right\rfloor
=a(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
For family \(1\), where \(d_1=\varphi\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_1(n)
&=\left\lfloor5\frac n\varphi\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\varphi\frac n\varphi\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor t\frac n\varphi\right\rfloor\\
&=\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{\varphi}\right\rfloor+n
 +\left\lfloor\frac{nt}{\varphi}\right\rfloor
=b(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, for family \(2\), where \(d_2=t\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_2(n)
&=\left\lfloor5\frac nt\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\varphi\frac nt\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor t\frac nt\right\rfloor\\
&=\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{t}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{n\varphi}{t}\right\rfloor+n
=c(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
All these ranks are positive: at \(v_i(n)\), the \(i\)-th floor summand equals \(n\ge1\), while the other summands are nonnegative.

We have proved that every positive integer \(p\) is some rank \(R_i(n)\), hence is a value of one of \(a,b,c\). Conversely, every value of any of the three sequences is such a positive rank. Thus the union of their ranges is exactly the set of positive integers. If a number lay in the ranges of two different sequences, it would give equal ranks \(R_i(n)=R_j(m)\) with \(i\ne j\), contradicting uniqueness of ranks. Therefore the three ranges are pairwise disjoint. Hence A207672, A207673, and A208326 partition the positive integers.
